item.title: Researcher examines how blood vessel damage relates to memory loss
item.description:

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a complex health issue with useful vocabulary and context

Researcher examines how blood vessel damage relates to memory loss

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Alzheimer's disease is often the focus when someone develops memory problems. But changes in the brain's blood vessels may also be part of the picture—and new research by the University of Kentucky's Cellas Hayes, Ph.D., helps explain why those changes deserve closer attention.

Hayes, an assistant professor who recently joined UK's Sanders-Brown Center on Aging, and his collaborators examined how different types of blood vessel damage relate to memory and thinking, and how much of those relationships could be explained by Alzheimer's-related brain changes.

Their findings, published in the journal Brain, point to an important distinction: While amyloid protein buildup in blood vessel walls was closely connected with Alzheimer's-related changes, thickening and hardening of the brain's small blood vessels remained linked to poorer thinking abilities even after researchers accounted for those changes.

"Different types of blood vessel damage may tell us different things about memory loss," Hayes said. "Understanding those differences could help researchers develop more complete approaches to dementia prevention and treatment."

Linking cognitive tests with brain examinations

The study used data from 1,269 people who participated in research at 34 Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers (ADRCs), including those at Sanders-Brown's ADRC. Participants completed tests of memory and thinking during their lives and donated their brains for examination after death. Their average age at death was 84.

Researchers compared participants' most recent test results with findings from their brain examinations. The tests assessed memory, the ability to use and understand words, and skills such as planning and problem-solving.

The team examined five types of blood vessel damage, including thickened small vessels, fatty deposits in larger arteries, protein buildup in vessel walls and areas of brain tissue damaged by interrupted blood flow. Their analyses accounted for differences in age, sex, education and a genetic factor associated with Alzheimer's risk.

Two vessel conditions show different patterns

Two forms of vessel disease stood out.

The first, called arteriolosclerosis, involves thickening and hardening of the brain's small blood vessels. About 41% of participants had moderate or severe changes of this type.

More severe small-vessel thickening was associated with poorer performance in memory, language, and planning and problem-solving. Although Alzheimer's-related changes explained part of those relationships in the researchers' statistical models, a substantial connection remained after those changes were taken into account.

"Blood vessel health is an important part of understanding memory loss," Hayes said. "In our study, damage to the brain's small blood vessels was linked to poorer memory and thinking even after accounting for Alzheimer's-related changes."

The second condition, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, occurs when amyloid protein builds up in blood vessel walls. About 56% of participants had these deposits.

Greater severity of this condition was also associated with poorer performance across all three thinking abilities. However, Alzheimer's-related changes accounted for a much larger share of those relationships—roughly 60% to 90%, depending on the thinking ability measured. These estimates describe relationships within the study's statistical models, rather than an individual person's risk of dementia.

Treatments may need to address multiple contributors

Together, the findings help distinguish conditions that often occur in the same brain but may have different relationships with memory and thinking.

That distinction could help guide future research into treatments that address several contributors to cognitive problems. Therapies focused on Alzheimer's-related changes alone may leave other sources of difficulty unaddressed, including changes to the vessels and blood flow in the brain.

"To develop more complete approaches to dementia, we need to understand the multiple types of damage that can occur in the same brain," Hayes said. "An important next question is whether addressing blood vessel disease alongside Alzheimer's-related changes can better preserve memory and thinking."

Causation and broader applicability remain uncertain

The study does not establish that blood vessel damage causes Alzheimer's disease or that treating it will prevent memory loss. Because the brain conditions were examined together after death, researchers could not determine which developed first.

The participants also represented a selected research population: Approximately 95% were white, their average education was 16 years and about 60% had dementia at their last assessment. Further studies are needed to determine whether the same patterns appear in more diverse populations.

Following people over time, while measuring blood vessel changes, Alzheimer's markers and thinking abilities, will be an important next step.

The findings connect with broader work underway in Hayes' laboratory at Sanders-Brown and UK's Department of Neuroscience. His team studies how blood markers of Alzheimer's disease and other brain changes evolve over time, alongside genetic research and investigations into how vascular health and social factors contribute to differences in brain aging. The goal is to identify opportunities to reduce risk, slow disease progression and develop more personalized approaches to care.

Hayes also emphasized the contributions of research participants and their families, whose decisions to donate made the study possible.

"Brain donation provides an extraordinary opportunity to understand what underlies memory and thinking problems," Hayes said. "This work reflects the generosity of participants and families who wanted to help future generations."

item.title: Researchers find teens are more likely to use tobacco, alcohol and marijuana when adults at home smoke or vape
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important research findings presented with clear detail and useful vocabulary

Researchers find teens are more likely to use tobacco, alcohol and marijuana when adults at home smoke or vape

Researchers from Children's Hospital of Philadelphia found that adolescents whose parents, caregivers or other adults at home use tobacco or e-cigarettes were substantially more likely to use tobacco, alcohol, marijuana and other substances and to screen positive for high-risk substance use. Rates were highest when both the parent and another adult in the home used these products. The findings were published in the journal Pediatrics.

Several prior studies confirmed that parental tobacco and e-cigarette use is a strong predictor of adolescent use. What was less known was whether the use of tobacco or e-cigarettes among parents and caregivers was associated with broader adolescent substance use.

Understanding the associations between household tobacco and e-cigarette use and teen substance use could help address risks related to adolescent tobacco, alcohol, marijuana and other substance use.

To help address this knowledge gap, researchers linked two sources of information already collected in the electronic health record (EHR) during routine visits across CHOP's Care Network between January 2025 and May 2026: parents' and caregivers' answers to tobacco screening questions from an automated tobacco treatment program, and adolescents' own answers on a confidential health questionnaire.

Rather than focus solely on tobacco and e-cigarette use, researchers explored whether adolescents were more likely to use other substances and potentially develop patterns of high-risk use, as measured by a validated adolescent screening tool.

"This study shows that household tobacco and e-cigarette use isn't just a parental health issue. It's a risk factor for adolescent substance use that pediatric clinicians can act on," said lead study author Brian Jenssen, MD, MSHP, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, a primary care pediatrician and medical director for value-based care for the CHOP Care Network, and associate director for clinical impact at Clinical Futures at CHOP.

The study analyzed data from 60,069 adolescents and found that nearly 1 in 4 adolescents (23.5%) used tobacco or nicotine products when both the parent or caregiver at the visit and another adult in the home used tobacco or e-cigarettes, compared with 13.5% when only the parent or caregiver used, 11.8% when only another adult in the home used and 2.0% when no one in the home used.

Similar patterns were observed with alcohol, marijuana and other substances. After accounting for age, sex, insurance and neighborhood opportunity, adolescents in homes where both a parent and another adult used tobacco or e-cigarettes had nearly 15 times the odds of screening positive for high-risk substance use as adolescents in homes with no use.

Parent vaping was not a lower-risk alternative for teens: in households where only the parent or caregiver used nicotine, adolescents with a parent who exclusively vaped had 5.6 times the odds of tobacco or nicotine use, compared with 2.6 times the odds among those whose parent only smoked, versus households with no use. This pattern held across most substances.

Because the study captured data at a single point in time, it cannot establish that household tobacco or e-cigarette use causes adolescent substance use; shared family, social and environmental factors may also play a role. Still, the consistent pattern across substances suggests household use is a practical risk signal for pediatric clinicians.

The EHR-integrated screening system that generated these data is currently used across CHOP, including all 31 CHOP Care Network practices, multiple subspecialty sites and both emergency departments. A parent's positive tobacco screen can trigger cessation support for the parent and alert clinicians to provide targeted substance-use prevention for the adolescent—addressing risk across two generations in a single visit.

"Every time a parent comes in for their child's checkup, we have an opportunity to protect not just one patient, but the whole family," Jenssen said. "This study shows we can use the data we already have to do exactly that."

item.title: Daily cannabis use surpasses daily drinking among Canadians under 50, survey finds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Significant public health trend with clear reporting and useful context

Daily cannabis use surpasses daily drinking among Canadians under 50, survey finds

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

Six years after cannabis legalization, more adults under 50 in Canada use cannabis daily than drink every day, and daily cannabis smoking is now as common as daily cigarette smoking for adults under age 35, according to new research in CMAJ (Canadian Medical Association Journal) .

"These shifts likely have profound implications for mental health, heart disease and lung health, and cancer risk that we are only beginning to understand," says Dr. Daniel Myran, the senior author, who is the Cheesbrough Research Chair at North York General, a clinician-scientist and associate professor at the University of Toronto's Department of Family and Community Medicine, and a scientist at ICES and the Bruyère Health Research Institute.

Over the last 20 years, cannabis use has increased in Canada and the United States, tobacco use has declined, and alcohol use has remained stable or declined in some groups. Canada legalized nonmedical cannabis in 2018, becoming the first country in the world to allow commercial retail sales and promotion.

In 2020, a wide variety of products with high tetrahydrocannabinol content, including vapes, edibles and concentrates, entered the legal market. While adolescent cannabis use has remained largely stable after legalization—though at some of the highest levels in the world—regular cannabis use has increased in adults.

Regular cannabis use has long been associated with addiction, psychosis and schizophrenia. Increasing evidence suggests it may be a risk factor for chronic disease, including heart attacks, strokes, lung disease and other mental health problems, and evidence is limited and mixed on cancer risk.

In this study, researchers looked at daily use of cannabis, alcohol and tobacco reported from almost 100,000 respondents to the 2023 to 2024 Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS).

Many previous studies have examined changes in cannabis use over time and have primarily looked at past-year use. This study examined daily use, a much stronger predictor of mental health and addiction. It also examined cannabis by mode of use and compared it to the regular use of other substances.

"This study suggests a generational shift in substance use behaviors has taken place, which will likely have long-term implications for population health," says lead author Dr. André McDonald, a psychiatric epidemiologist and Canadian Institutes of Health Research postdoctoral fellow at McMaster University's Peter Boris Center for Addictions Research, Hamilton, Ontario.

"Declining cigarette use among younger people reflects long-term tobacco-control policies, changing social norms and greater awareness of harms. Conversely, increases in cannabis use are consistent with greater availability, social acceptability and normalization in the postlegalization era."

"One of the most surprising findings was that a substantial number of people who use cannabis daily don't drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes every day," says Myran.

"Only 11.2% of people who use cannabis daily also drink alcohol daily, while only 38.4% also smoke cigarettes daily. It is commonly assumed that regular cannabis smoking goes hand in hand with tobacco use, but that didn't appear to be the case for almost two-thirds of people who use cannabis daily."

Effect of legalization

"Canada is the first country in the world to create a commercial retail market with a wide variety of product offerings and product promotion. To me, many of the patterns of cannabis use that are emerging in Canada's mature legal market offer a strong caution to other countries around the world about the potential harms of this approach," says Myran.

"One of the arguments for legalization and increasing the variety of products on the market is that it would shift people away from smoked cannabis toward other forms of use, like edibles, that may have lower risk for heart or lung disease or cancer. These findings don't really support that occurring; in people who use cannabis daily, 68% continue to report smoking as the main method of use."

Cannabis legalization had a major impact on consumption patterns, with 41% of adults who used cannabis daily reporting they began doing so after legalization. More than half of females using cannabis daily (51.2%) reported starting daily cannabis use after legalization. This proportion was 85.4% for younger adults (ages 18 to 24 years) using cannabis daily.

"Policy efforts have historically focused on reducing alcohol and tobacco use, and for good reason. Our findings suggest high-frequency cannabis use needs to be considered a priority alongside them. Over 1.8 million Canadians now use cannabis daily, of whom 750,000 began doing so after legalization. Given the health risks involved, preventing and reducing cannabis use has become a pressing public health issue," adds McDonald.

In places like Canada where cannabis is legal, the authors suggest tactics such as stronger communications about risk, marketing and retail restrictions, an increased minimum legal age, and targeted prevention and harm-reduction strategies to reduce usage in younger adults and vulnerable populations.

Publication details

Daily cannabis, alcohol, and cigarette use in Canada: results from the 2023 to 2024 Canadian Community Health Survey, Canadian Medical Association Journal (2026). DOI: 10.1503/cmaj.260962

Journal information: Canadian Medical Association Journal

item.title: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Innovative approach to health screening with clear explanation and useful vocabulary

Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out

- Published

Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.

AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.

Recruitment to the EDITH trial , externalhas already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.

Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.

At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.

About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.

It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

Prof Fiona Gilbert, department of radiology, University of Cambridge, honorary consultant at Addenbrooke's Hospital, and co-chief investigator said: "Millions of women have a mammogram each year and only a small number, less than 1%, will have cancer.

"Technology can make reviewing these images more efficient, freeing up specialist breast radiologists to spend more time caring for patients with cancer, supporting faster diagnosis and earlier treatment."

Gilbert told the BBC there was a "huge shortfall" in radiologists and that the number of imaging examinations was increasing by 8% a year.

Screening 'saved my life'

Shirley Essex, 70, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer a year ago after a routine screening appointment.

She had surgery and radiotherapy, but did not require chemotherapy.

She told the BBC that her mammogram had saved her life: "I was astonished to be told I had cancer because I did not have any symptoms."

Shirley is not part of the study but is passionate about the importance of screening.

"I feel so lucky my cancer was detected early. It was my last routine mammogram, so if I had not attended, my cancer would have kept growing," she said.

How will the trial work?

Women will be informed about the study when they receive a routine screening invitation, but will not be obliged to take part.

The trial will not change what happens during a breast screening appointment.

Instead, it will test whether AI-assisted tools could replace one of the two human specialists reviewing mammograms.

Researchers say machine-learning software can be trained on millions of previous images in order to detect patterns, and so potentially find subtle changes in breast tissue that might be missed by the human eye.

In one arm of the trial, an AI programme will grade images before they are sent to NHS experts. In another, it will review images afterwards.

The Â£11m trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).

It is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working with NHS England.

'Huge potential'

On a visit to the breast screening unit at Addenbrooke's Hospital, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper told the BBC: "AI has huge potential to improve treatment, which is why we need trials like this to ensure we are using it in the most effective way with proper safeguards."

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said NHS breast screening "saves lives" and he urged every woman invited to the trial to take part.

"Every scan will still be seen by a specialist, and if proven effective, it could ensure women get the diagnosis and treatment they need sooner," he said.

Four AI companies are involved in the trial, which is expected to last around three years.
